meeting_header:
Date: 2026-06-17 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Ruiz (Bridgewell Head of ML), Ellen Park (Platform Lead), Marcus Lee (Security)
summary: Discovery to validate p95 latency targets and throughput for streaming conversational use-case. Bridgewell is evaluating hosted vs private deployment due to PII and latency constraints. Agreed to run token/sec benchmarks and end-to-end streaming p95 checks; Redwood to provide harness and initial config recommendations.
topics: Objectives and success criteria (p95 targets, cost ceilings)
Current infra and request patterns (burst concurrency, average vs tail)
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs (data residency, KMS, SLOs)
Benchmark plan: token/sec, streaming p95, cold-starts, prefix caching
Security/compliance questions (SOC2, audit logs, SSO/SAML, KMS)
transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros?
[00:00:08] Daniel: Hey, Daniel Ruiz here, I run ML at Bridgewell. Our team is trying to nail down p95 for streaming chat and decide whether to go hosted or private.
[00:00:18] Ellen: Ellen Park, platform. We're responsible for infra and latency SLOs for customer-facing flows.
[00:00:22] Marcus: Marcus Lee, security - I'll keep the compliance questions coming.
[00:00:26] Alex: Great, from Redwood Priya (SE) and I, we'll go through what we typically measure and then dig into your numbers.
[00:00:35] Priya: quick note, audio might cut a bit, I have some slides but i'll keep it conversational.
[00:00:42] Alex: First, can you give us your p95 target and what a failure looks like?
[00:00:48] Daniel: We aim for p95 < 250ms for token streaming on short-turn dialogs (~30-80 tokens). For longer responses up to 512 tokens we want p95 < 600ms per chunk, but the user experience metric is end-to-end response within 1.2s for most. If that slips we get churn.
[00:01:08] Ellen: And concurrency, burst patterns: we see steady 50 rps in prod, but spikes up to 120 concurrent streaming sessions for short windows. Also background batch jobs generate occasional KV warmups.
[00:01:22] Priya: ok, so 250ms p95 for short is tight but in our hosted low-latency profiles we can often hit 200-300ms with continuous batching and prefix caching — depending on model size and tokenization. Are you running an open model or custom fine-tune?
[00:01:40] Daniel: We're on a trimmed open LLM with a small fine-tune and a 1.2B-ish footprint in quantized form. We also have heavier flights where we call external retrieval before generation — that's another 100-150ms occasionally.
[00:01:53] Alex: Good to call out retrieval. For benchmarking we'll need traces that show the end-to-end breakdown: network, retrieval, model decode.
[00:02:02] Marcus: On security, we can't send raw customer PII to third-party hosted services unencrypted. We need KMS integration and audit logs; SOC2 Type II is required. Can Redwood hosted accommodate that?
[00:02:15] Priya: short answer: yes, our hosted tier offers envelope encryption with customer-managed keys and audit logs, but for our largest enterprise customers we recommend Dedicated or Private with a VPC peering option to reduce egress and to keep logs inside your control.
[00:02:31] Ellen: And what about predictable throughput? If we reserve capacity, what's the scaling behavior on burst?
[00:02:37] Alex: With Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools with configurable burst capacity. We can size a pool to sustain your 120 concurrent streaming sessions with headroom; autoscaling adds more but you pay for that burst. Private gives you full control over capacity and network pathing which usually reduces jitter.
[00:02:54] [00:03:00] (Speaker overlap) Daniel: I think key for us is the p95 during that 120 concurrent spike window — we saw previous vendors drop to 800-900ms in the tail during spikes.
[00:03:12] Priya: Understood. For the token/sec benchmarking we'll measure: cold start latency, steady-state token/sec per GPU, per-request p95 for streaming chunks, and end-to-end tail including retrieval.
[00:03:25] Alex: We'll propose a harness that mimics your request traces. We'll need sample trace files (timestamps, tokens/turn, retrieval times).
[00:03:33] Daniel: we can share anonymized traces. How do you simulate the client-side streaming?
[00:03:38] Priya: we have a streaming client shim that replays the same chunk sizes and client-side backpressure. It inserts jitter to match real-world networks. That said, sometimes the transcription here might show "K-V cache" as "KV cash" ha — apologies, our automated notes get fuzzy.
[00:03:55] Marcus: Regarding keys: we require KMS with HSM-backed keys and rotation policy. Also need to ensure that any logs with PII are redacted or held in our VPC.
[00:04:05] Alex: For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and all logs remain in their environment. For hosted we offer options but agree the Private path is cleaner for strict controls.
[00:04:15] Ellen: Costly though. We have a $X/token ceiling for hosted, otherwise we need to justify Dedicated CAPEX.
[00:04:22] Alex: We'll include cost projections in the follow-up—tokens/sec impacts GPU utilization directly; higher batching reduces cost per token but can increase latency. We'll show trade-off curves.
[00:04:32] [00:04:40] Daniel: Can you explain batching mechanics? We worry about batching delaying first tokens in streaming.
[00:04:45] Priya: Sure. Redwood supports continuous batching and priority lanes. Streaming requests can be routed to a low-latency lane with minimal batching (e.g., micro-batch size 1-2) to keep per-token latency low; bulk non-interactive requests go to a batch-optimized lane. There's also prefix/KV caching that can short-circuit much of the compute for repeated contexts.
[00:05:05] Ellen: That sounds useful — we have a lot of similar prompts across sessions. How effective is KV cache in practice?
[00:05:11] Priya: Depends on prompt reuse and sequence overlap. In our customers we've seen 20-60% token compute reduction with effective prefix caching on conversational flows.
[00:05:20] Marcus: A compliance question — do you persist KV cache to disk, and where is that stored?
[00:05:25] Alex: Caches are stored in encrypted store; for Private deployments that store can be in your VPC. For Hosted it's in our managed infrastructure with encryption at rest and role-based ACLs.
[00:05:35] [00:05:50] Daniel: For the benchmark, we're most concerned about the p95 of streaming on the tail of bursts. Can you run a sustained 10-minute spike at 120 concurrent and show p50/p95/p99?
[00:05:58] Priya: Yes. We'll run sustained and pulsed workloads: a 10-minute steady spike and a repeated short-peak pattern. We'll capture token/sec per GPU, p95 per chunk, and p99 cold starts.
[00:06:10] Alex: Also useful: capture the distribution of sequence lengths, since kernel selection changes perf.
[00:06:14] Daniel: We'll include that.
[00:06:20] Ellen: Ok, what's the timeline for a pilot? We want a two-week pilot ideally.
[00:06:24] Alex: If we get traces by mid-week, we can run benchmarks and share results within 3-4 business days. Pilot kickoff week of 6/29 is realistic.
[00:06:33] Marcus: Security handshake — we'll need an NDA addendum and a SOC2 packet.
[00:06:38] Alex: We'll attach SOC2 + security whitepaper. Priya will add KMS and private options doc.
[00:06:44] [00:07:00] (Background noise) Daniel: one more question on model variants: can Redwood route to smaller quantized variants on burst to keep latency bounded?
[00:07:09] Priya: Yes, routing policies can fallback to smaller quantized model variants or lower-precision runtimes when capacity constrained. We can do A/B tests and automatic fallback rules. There is a quality tradeoff — we'll show evals vs latency curves.
[00:07:22] Ellen: And telemetry? We need token-level breakdowns per route and ability to set alerts on p95 regressions.
[00:07:29] Alex: The Console exposes per-route token/latency/cost breakdowns and tracing hooks. You can set regression alerts tied to prompt-set evals.
[00:07:37] [00:07:50] Priya: quick real-world example: a customer had a 30% token reduction after switching to prefix cache and tuned batching — we reduced p95 by 30ms and saved ~20% in cost.
[00:07:58] Daniel: Sounds promising. I'd like to see numbers for a 1.2B quantized model on gpus similar to A100/NVIDIA-like profiles.
[00:08:07] Priya: we'll include both A100-equivalent and cheaper TPU/GPU mix profiles for cost tradeoffs. Note though some kernels behave differently on different hardware — we capture that in our kernel-selection matrix.
[00:08:20] Ellen: Is there an easy way to reproduce the benchmark locally before sending traces?
[00:08:25] Alex: We'll provide a dockerized harness that can run in your env or ours. The harness replays traces and reports p50/p95/p99 and token/sec.
[00:08:33] Marcus: On retention, how long do you keep logs for hosted pilot? We need 90-day retention in our policy.
[00:08:38] Priya: Hosted default is 30 days but we can extend retention for pilot enterprise accounts; for Private you control retention entirely.
[00:08:45] [00:09:00] Daniel: Any caveats on cold-starts for streaming? Some vendors had big initial latency until KV warmed.
[00:09:06] Priya: cold starts depend on model warm state and KV cache. We recommend a lightweight warmup traffic pattern before business hours. Also we have warm pools to reduce instance spin-up for Dedicated.
[00:09:17] Alex: We'll measure cold/steady-start delta in the benchmark.
[00:09:21] Ellen: What about throttling policies? During large bursts, do you gracefully degrade by falling back to non-streaming responses?
[00:09:29] Priya: You can configure fallback policies: queue, throttle, or return shorter responses / fewer tokens. We usually recommend canary rules coupled with A/B evaluation so you can measure UX impact.
[00:09:40] [00:10:00] Daniel: Ok, let's talk numbers — for our trial what throughput should we request? We're thinking reserve enough for 150 concurrent to be safe.
[00:10:08] Alex: For 150 concurrent streaming sessions at average 40 tokens per second across sessions, that's ~6k tokens/sec sustained — we'll translate that into GPU counts in the plan. We'll include both conservative (150) and optimistic (120) sizing.
[00:10:22] Priya: FYI token/sec per GPU depends on batch config and model size; for a 1.2B quantized model you might see 6k-12k tokens/sec per high-end GPU in steady-state with optimized kernels. We'll provide measured numbers.
[00:10:35] Ellen: That range helps. Can you annotate the plan with expected latencies at different token/sec points?
[00:10:40] Alex: yes, trade-off curves.
[00:10:43] [00:11:00] Marcus: Another checklist: SAML SSO, SCIM, RBAC, audit logs delivery to Splunk — supported?
[00:11:08] Priya: supported. For Hosted we integrate with SAML and can push audit logs to your SIEM; for Private it's native access.
[00:11:15] Daniel: Great. A few small points: our dev team wants an API that mirrors your hosted SDK for private as well.
[00:11:22] Alex: That's a core Redwood design — same API surface across hosting modes.
[00:11:26] Priya: also will include recommended quantization settings — 4-bit vs 8-bit tradeoffs and effect on p95.
[00:11:33] [00:11:50] Ellen: What's the acceptance criteria for pilot success?
[00:11:54] Daniel: if p95 < 300ms for short-turns during 10-min spike and cost is within our ceiling, we greenlight Dedicated or Private procurement.
[00:12:04] Alex: we'll use that as a gating metric.

  [00:12:15] (silence)
  [00:20:05] Priya: jumping back in — some technical clarifications: application-side retries can amplify load due to backoff misconfig. If you have aggressive client retries, we recommend client-side token-aware throttling.
  [00:20:22] Daniel: noted. We'll audit our client retry behavior.
  [00:30:02] Alex: quick callout on telemetry sampling — we recommend full token-level metrics during pilot, then sample in steady-state to save retention costs.
  [00:40:10] Priya: we're drafting the benchmark plan now — it will include: workload replay, cold-start measurements, sustained spike, pulsed bursts, sequence length histogram, and model variant A/B.
  [00:45:00] Ellen: for the pilot harness, can it run inside our gcp project so network egress is representative?
  [00:45:08] Priya: yes, we can run the harness in your VPC or run it from Redwood's region with VPC peering. We'll document both.
  [00:47:15] Marcus: let's be explicit on who owns data during the pilot — metadata, traces, anonymization.
  [00:47:22] Alex: we'll add a short data handling addendum to the NDA.
  [00:49:00] Daniel: ok makes sense. I'm comfortable moving forward with the benchmark.
  [00:49:10] Alex: recap of next steps: we'll send the benchmark harness + plan, security packet, and pricing estimates; Bridgewell to provide anonymous traces and KMS requirements.
  [00:49:25] Ellen: we'll aim to get traces and requirements by Friday.
  [00:49:30] Priya: we'll schedule the pilot kickoff in the shared calendar for the week of 6/29.
  [00:49:36] Marcus: I'll review the SOC2 packet when it's sent.
  [00:49:40] Alex: thanks everyone, speak soon.
  [00:49:45] (meeting ends)
questions: Can Redwood hosted meet KMS and SOC2 constraints for PII?
What's the expected p95 delta between hosted and private for quantized 1.2B models?
How does prefix/KV caching reduce token compute in conversational flows?
Can we simulate realistic client-side streaming and backpressure in the benchmark harness?
